title: Papa Celestin, Sam Morgan, Johnny Dave and Willie Pajeaud
summary: After the Hummingbird he joined Celestin, then Sam Morgan's band on the road, fought Johnny Dave for the banjo chair, and later played jitney dances with Pajeaud.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs

blocks.x: Yes, very good. All right, let's see. Can you tell us a little bit more about your first days? How long did you stay there at the Hummingbird, and where did you go after that?

Well, I stood at the Hummingbird for about, I'll say, about nine months. And one night, John had some misunderstanding in the band, and to my surprise, Papa Salistad called me in the band. I was just that good. My name had began to spread, you see, because the cabaret used to open at night. But in the daytime, they had plenty of advertisement, plenty of jobs at Millenburg, all that in the day. So I was gigging with Rene, Buddy Petit, Chris, and all them outside, and my name began to spread. That guy plays a good banjo. He's a good banjo player, you know. Chris Kelly, I remember him. Tell me I was the greatest banjo player in the world. Play on the job all day. Give me 50 cents. You're going to make it. You're going to make it. I said, and that's just, he just bullshitted me with that. But God knows I love, but I was going to make it, you know. Well, I mean, thank God. I finally did make it, too. You know what I mean? So I went to work with Salistad, and I stood with him, say, about a year. And one day I was sitting at home. We was living at 627 North Johnson. We're between St. Pete and Old Basin now, which is a part of the housing project. All that's gone now. And a big fella come to the door, all dressed up in the tuxi, knock at the door, and ask mama for me. And I come to the door, he says, are you George? I said, yes. He said, well, I'm Sam Morgan. Man, Sam Morgan, that sounded like Duke Ellington to me, you know, because them cats was really insane then. And they was playing in all the hotels and all the cool. And what I wanted to do, I was satisfied with Salistad, but Salistad wasn't doing plenty traveling. And a guy told me he was going to Mobile. That looked like he was going to Hindustan or somewhere. I'd never been across the street in my life, you see. So when he said we're going to play Mobile and all that, man, that sounded like going to New York or something. So he asked me, did I want to go on the road with him? So I said, yeah, I'll go on the road with you. So I went on the road, and I ate that dust out there. And, man, I went through all the hardships they had out there with him. And that leads to another question. You see, Johnny Dave was that regular banjo player. So I went on the road. You didn't tell me nothing about Johnny Dave. So I'd have net up all that dust and everything out there, and I'm getting better and better, though. I'm getting so that I'm able to take all them pretty one-string solos and all them kind of things. So we're going to play a job. Sam's got a job playing on the Temple Roof Garden. I'm me. I come on to the job. All I found out the job was going to be, say, Monday or Tuesday. I come up there all dressed up. When I got up there, Mr. Johnny Dave was standing there. He looked at me and said, well, that's all right, boy. I'm taking over tonight, and you know me. You know me. I've been that way ever since I was 12 years old. Who's taking over tonight, you know? So I look at him, and they say, yeah, Johnny's going to play. I say, well, okay, man. I said, Johnny's going to play. I took him down the corner, and I come home. Laid across the bed, barely crying like a baby. You know what I mean? Yeah, all because the roof garden was the big thing them days, all them pretty girls and everything up there. And I can play. I know I can play, and I want to play for them, but I'm denied that right. So I didn't say nothing. I went home. About three days after, yeah, he come knock on the door. So we're going to pass Chris Dan or something. I say, you're going to pass Chris Dan, not me. I say, man, don't never come here and ask me to play with y'all no more. I say, man, of all the things. I say, who do he think he is? I say, I play more with one hand tied behind my back than he ever could play with all that big talk he got. So I say, now y'all going to have to make a choice. Either it's going to be Johnny Dave playing banjo with you, or I'm going to play. I say, because I ain't going nowhere with you. Well, he wanted me bad, you know what I mean? So and so, well, they called the band to a meeting, and all the gang voted me in and voted this cat out. So he passed the rumor. The first time I find him playing somewhere, I'm going to go up there and run him out the joint. So we went on the road about three weeks after we gets a job at the Santa Center Club. And yeah, he walks in the door with his banjo. And when he walked in the door, he was playing a number. I'll never forget it. Think of me thinking of you. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. So when I seen him coming in the door, I made everybody get down with me in my rhythm. And I went to picking him. So, dun-dun-dun-dun-dun-dun-dun.
